Voice processing

Last updated 17 October 2026

On this page
  • Your microphone
  • What you hear
  • Your camera's background
  • Live captions

How Iskra cleans up your microphone and what you hear, blurs or replaces your camera's background, captions what people say, and translates messages. Everything runs on your own device: the models and engines ship inside the app (and the web app, from its own address), audio and video are processed in your browser or desktop app, and no sound, picture, transcript or model input is sent anywhere for processing. Nothing about it is logged or stored, apart from your settings on this device, the flags that remember when this device was too slow for AI noise removal or a background effect, and the speech and translation models kept on the device so they're only downloaded once.

Your microphone#

Setting (Settings → Voice & audio → Noise suppression) What runs
AI DeepFilterNet3, a neural network, as WebAssembly in a Web Worker fed by an AudioWorklet at 48 kHz
Strong (default) RNNoise, as WebAssembly in an AudioWorklet at 48 kHz
Standard The browser's own noise suppression
Off Nothing
  • Fallbacks. AI needs AudioWorklet and WebAssembly with SIMD. If those are missing, the engine can't start, or it runs slower than real time for three seconds in a row (realtime factor above 0.6), or its worker is late for more than a quarter of each second three seconds in a row (a late frame now and then only costs a short crossfade), Iskra switches to RNNoise by itself and remembers it on that device. The developer console says why. Choosing AI again gives it another try. RNNoise falls back to the browser's suppression the same way. Settings always says which engine is active, why, and (in a call) how much CPU it takes.
  • AI noise removal strength (Settings → Voice & audio, with AI on): Gentle, Normal (default) or Max: the most DeepFilterNet may turn anything down (18 dB, 30 dB, no limit). With a limit, what it takes out is mixed back in at that level, so noise stays far down and a wrong guess about the voice can only cost that much. Iskra runs DeepFilterNet with the local SNR thresholds its own command line tool uses (-15, 35, 35 dB: both stages on every frame); libDF's WebAssembly defaults (-10, 30, 20) skipped stages frame by frame and turned clean speech down by about 9 dB, choppily (see "How transparent it is" below). Changes apply right away, in a call too.
  • Automatic gain. The browser's automatic gain control is off by default when Strong or AI runs (it pumps the level under the noise removal), and on with Standard or Off. Settings → Voice & audio lets you choose either way.
  • Voice activity. With "Set automatically" on, Silero VAD (a small neural network, run in plain TypeScript in the same AudioWorklet) decides when you're speaking: the mic opens when it hears speech and stays open through pauses for 500 ms (hangover). It keeps the last 100 ms and sends them when it opens (pre-roll), so the start of a word isn't cut off. That makes you 100 ms late for as long as you keep talking; the gate never skips or squeezes audio to catch up (that sounds choppy and hurried). Silero notices a word 25–40 ms after its voiced part starts, so that always gets through; it notices the faintest lead-in (a breath or soft consonant 20–30 dB down) up to 145 ms after it starts, so that is now and then softened, by 15–30 ms typically and 45 ms at most on the test phrases (a longer pre-roll of 200 ms would keep all of it, at twice the delay). After a pause of more than the hangover it closes, and the next time starts over. In noise Silero is sure of a soft first sound later, so the gate already opens at a probability of 0.2 and closes again if Silero doesn't reach 0.5 within 200 ms (no added delay; noise alone hardly ever opens it). Turn "Set automatically" off for a manual volume threshold instead. Push-to-talk is never gated or delayed. Your own speaking ring follows the same detector.
  • Off the audio thread. The audio worklet only moves samples: it cuts the mic into 10 ms frames for a worker that runs DeepFilterNet, and plays what comes back at a fixed delay, the way DeepFilterNet's own LADSPA plugin uses a processing thread. Frames travel in eight slots allocated once and reused (nothing is allocated per frame on the audio thread): buffers transferred back and forth over a MessagePort, or shared memory with Atomics when the page is cross-origin isolated (none of the apps are today: the web app, the desktop app's app:// and the phone apps all use the port; the choice is made at run time). If a frame isn't back in time, the worklet crossfades (2.7 ms) to the mic as it is, lined up to the same delay, and back once frames arrive again: never silence, never a skip or a repeat. A frame that couldn't be sent at all also takes the next three with it (the network's look-ahead still held audio from before the gap).
  • Latency added. DeepFilterNet: 24 ms of framing and queue (one frame, plus one device buffer of headroom for the worker: the delay follows the device's buffer size, 24 ms for the usual 10 ms) plus the model's own look-ahead (30 ms), 54 ms in all; running inside the audio worklet it was 10.7 + 30 ms, with no room for a slow frame. RNNoise: about 10 ms. Voice activity: 100 ms while you talk ("Set automatically" only; none with a manual threshold or push-to-talk).
  • Hi-fi. In voice channels where an admin allowed it, turning on "Hi-fi audio" sends your mic in stereo at 128 kbps with no noise suppression, echo cancellation or automatic gain. Use headphones.
  • Resilience. The mic is published with Opus in-band FEC, RED (redundant audio: each packet also carries the previous ones, so a lost packet costs nothing) and DTX (next to nothing is sent while you're quiet). LiveKit's default codecs include audio/red, so every room negotiates it.

What you hear#

Where the app mixes call audio with Web Audio (Chrome, Edge, the desktop app; not Safari or Firefox), each incoming voice goes through:

  1. Clean up others' audio (off by default): DeepFilterNet3 when you use AI noise removal and up to four people are talking, RNNoise otherwise or when the device can't keep up. DeepFilterNet runs in a Web Worker, so starting it for someone who just joined never stalls the rest of the call; it uses the same queue as the mic (24 ms on top of the model's look-ahead, crossfading to the voice as it is when the worker falls behind). It runs at the Normal strength. Clips record the cleaned voices while this is on.
  2. Even out voices (on by default): a slow gain that brings each person towards the same loudness (only while they talk, at most ±12 dB, at most 3 dB per second, gliding sample by sample), then a gentle compressor (2:1 above -16 dBFS RMS, 10 ms attack, 200 ms release: only syllables well above the target) and a look-ahead limiter at -1 dBFS (it sees peaks 1.5 ms ahead and ramps down over that time, so it never clips or steps). Adds 1.5 ms.
  3. Your per-person volume, on top.

Your camera's background#

Settings → Camera: Off (default), Blur, or Replace with a built-in picture (Aurora, Sunset: soft gradients drawn by the app, nothing to download) or a solid colour. The preview there runs exactly what calls run.

  • What runs. MediaPipe's Selfie Segmenter (a 256×256 person-segmentation network, run by MediaPipe Tasks in WebAssembly on the CPU) finds you in each frame, in a Web Worker. The mask is smoothed over time (quick to follow real movement, slow to flicker) and feathered at the edges, then WebGL2 in the same worker draws you over a blurred copy of the frame (you are left out of the blur, so you don't bleed into it), the picture or the colour.
  • Off the main thread. In Chrome, Edge and the desktop app the camera's frames stream into the worker and back out (insertable streams), so the page never touches them and a hidden tab keeps going. Other browsers send frames to the worker as images.
  • Nothing of the room first. In a call the effect is in place before the camera is published, and until the first mask is ready the whole frame counts as background.
  • Fallback. Needs WebAssembly and WebGL2 in workers. If the effect can't start, or the device can't keep up (fewer than 10 frames a second, or more than 60 ms a frame, for three 2-second windows in a row), it turns itself off with a notice in the call ("your real background is showing") and remembers that on this device until you choose an effect again. In a call, Settings shows the frame rate and time per frame; the app logs them to the developer console every 10 seconds.
  • Library telemetry. Newer MediaPipe Tasks releases (1.x) send usage statistics to Google; Iskra uses 0.10.35, which has none, and the workers that run on-device models can only fetch from the app's own address anyway.

Live captions#

Opt in per listener: the captions button in the call, or Settings → Voice & audio → Captions ("Show captions in calls"). Off by default. Each speaker's last words show under their name above the call controls (read out by screen readers as a polite live region); the × or the button turns them off again.

  • What runs. Each incoming voice (and yours, with "Caption my own voice too") is tapped in an AudioContext of its own (the cleaned-up voice when "Clean up others' audio" is on), resampled to 16 kHz in an AudioWorklet and sent to a captions Web Worker. There Silero VAD (the same model as for your mic) cuts it into phrases (200 ms pre-roll, ends after 500 ms of quiet, at most 8 s, at least 300 ms of speech), so only speech is ever transcribed. Whisper base (OpenAI's model, 8-bit ONNX export) transcribes one phrase at a time with ONNX Runtime Web (WebAssembly, one thread): greedy decoding, no timestamps, Whisper's own "no speech" and confidence checks, and a stop for runaway repeats. The feature extraction and decoding loop are Iskra's own TypeScript (client/src/state/captions/).
  • Languages. English and Swedish. "Automatic" lets Whisper pick between the two for each phrase; or fix one. Whisper base is good in English and usable but rough in Swedish.
  • Why Whisper base. It's MIT licensed (code and weights), speaks Swedish, and is the smallest Whisper that's worth reading (tiny is about twice as fast but much worse, in Swedish especially). Moonshine is faster on short phrases but English-only under a permissive license. Whisper always looks at 30 s of audio, so each phrase costs about the same no matter how short; WebGPU and multi-threading (which needs cross-origin isolation the app can't have) would make it much faster and are left for later.
  • Keeping up. One phrase at a time; at most 4 waiting and 3 people at once; a phrase that waited more than 8 s is skipped. Skipping 3 within 20 s, or one phrase taking more than 7 s, pauses captions for 20 s with "Captions paused: this device is too slow right now" and then tries again.
  • Privacy. The text exists only in this page's memory: it's shown, kept for 8 seconds after the last words, and dropped. It is never sent to the server or to anyone, never stored, never logged, and not part of clips.
  • Where the model comes from: your own server. Whisper base (78 MB: encoder, decoder and vocabulary) is not part of the app and not in git. The first time captions turn on in a call, the app says "Captions need a one-time 78 MB download from this server" and waits for Download; progress shows with a Cancel button. The parts come from the Iskra server the call runs on (GET /models/whisper-base-1846881b/<part>, on the web, in the desktop app and in the phone apps alike), with a short-lived link the app gets from the server first, so only members can download it (PROTOCOL.md). That server fetched the model once from Hugging Face, at the pinned commit, the first time anyone asked, and keeps it in its world folder (models/). So members' devices only ever talk to their own server; Hugging Face only sees the server's address, once. An owner can turn this off (Captions.ModelDownload in server.json, Hosting reference); the app then says "This server doesn't offer captions".
  • Hash check, twice. The server checks every file and part against the SHA-256s pinned in client/src/state/captions/model.json (compiled into both the server and the app) before keeping anything, and the app checks every part again before it's used or kept, and when it's read back. A part that doesn't match is refused ("wasn't the right file"); a failed download says so with Try again. Either way the call goes on untouched.
  • Kept on the device in Cache Storage (iskra-models), or IndexedDB where Cache Storage can't keep it (the desktop app's app://), under a key that doesn't depend on the server: one download per device, whichever server it came from. Files from an older version are removed.
  • Privacy. Getting the model is an ordinary file request to your own server. No audio, text or anything about the call goes with it, and the workers that run the models can't fetch anything at all.

Message translation#

Translate in a message's menu (channels, threads, DMs and group DMs; press and hold on a phone) shows the message in your language under the original: "Translated from Swedish · Show original". The translation button in a conversation's header turns on Auto-translate messages not in my language there, and picks the language to translate into (your app language unless you choose another; also in My settings → Language).

  • On your device, after decryption. It runs in a Web Worker on the text your app already shows, so it works for end-to-end encrypted channels, DMs and groups too. No message text is sent anywhere: not to your server, not to any translation service. Translations live only in the page's memory and are gone when the app closes.
  • Which language. ELD (n-grams, its smallest database, under 1 MB, bundled) tells the language on the device. Links, mentions, emoji, code and numbers don't count; a few letters ("lol", "ok") aren't enough, and auto-translate only acts when it's sure. On a close call between similar languages (Swedish, Danish, Norwegian) your own language wins, so your own messages stay untouched.
  • The engine. Bergamot, the WebAssembly translation engine of Firefox Translations (5 MB, bundled; client/vendor/bergamot, made by scripts/vendor-bergamot.mjs from the npm release, checked by its SHA-512), runs Mozilla's Firefox Translations models on the CPU: a chat message takes 10-150 ms. Plain text in and out, never HTML.
  • Languages. English to and from Swedish, Danish, Norwegian (Bokmål), Finnish, German, French, Spanish, Italian, Dutch, Portuguese, Polish and Ukrainian (client/src/state/translate/models.json, written by scripts/translate-pins.mjs from Mozilla's model registry: released models only). Between two other languages it goes through English (Swedish → English → German) in one step.
  • Why Bergamot. Its models are small because they're made for CPUs in browsers: 14-26 MB per direction as downloaded (17-32 MB unpacked), against about 110 MB for an Opus-MT model run with Transformers.js and ONNX Runtime, and they're faster. Mozilla keeps training and releasing them for Firefox. Code and models are MPL-2.0, so any server owner may pass them on.
  • Where the models come from: your own server. They aren't part of the app and not in git. An owner offers them in Server settings → Translation (off by default; it shows what each language weighs). The first time you translate from a language this device doesn't have, the message says what it needs ("Translating from Swedish needs a one-time 15 MB download from your server", with a word about mobile data on a phone) and waits for Download. The parts come from one of your servers that offers them (GET /models/translate/<dir>/<part>, with a short-lived members-only link; PROTOCOL.md). That server fetched that one model from Mozilla's storage the first time a member needed it, and keeps it in models/translate/: only languages members use are ever fetched, and Mozilla only sees the server's address. If none of your servers offers translation, Translate says so.
  • Hash checks. The server checks every file and part against the SHA-256s pinned in models.json (compiled into both), the app checks every part again, unpacks it (gzip) and checks the unpacked file too. Anything that doesn't match is refused and never used or kept.
  • Kept on the device in Cache Storage (iskra-translate-models), or IndexedDB where it can't (the desktop app), under a key that doesn't depend on the server: one download per language and direction per device. Models of an older version are removed.

Voice message transcripts#

Show transcript (the lines button on a voice message's player, in channels, encrypted channels, DMs and group DMs) shows what was said under the player. Settings → Voice & audio → Speech → Transcribe voice messages automatically (off by default) does it for every voice message you see.

  • The captions model, on your device. It's the same Whisper base model and worker as live captions, downloaded the same way (once, from your own server, after Download, SHA-256 checked, kept on the device). The app decodes the recording itself (the browser's own decoder, to 16 kHz mono), Silero VAD finds the speech, and the phrases are packed into as few 30-second Whisper windows as they fit. English and Swedish, as set for captions.
  • Never uploaded. Neither the recording (which the app already has) nor the text leaves the device. Transcripts of channel voice messages are kept in IndexedDB (iskra-transcripts, at most 2000, the oldest dropped first) so they don't have to be made again; transcripts of end-to-end encrypted voice messages are kept in memory only and are gone when the app closes. Signing out deletes them.
  • Too slow. If a transcript takes more than four times the recording's length (at least a minute), it stops with "This device took too long" and automatic transcripts stop on that device (asking still works; turning the setting off and on tries again). Browsers that can't run captions can't transcribe either and say so.

Read aloud#

Read aloud in a message's menu reads it with the device's own speech voices (speechSynthesis: Windows, macOS and iOS voices; speech-dispatcher on Linux). A channel's menu has Read new messages aloud (for gaming: a speaker button in the header shows it's on and turns it off). Messages sent with /tts <text> are read aloud for people who turned on Settings → Voice & audio → Speech → Play /tts messages (off by default); sending them needs the sendTts permission (admins have it; others get it from a role).

  • What's read. The author's name and the message as plain words: mentions by name, custom emoji by name, links as their host names ("link to github.com"), code blocks named, not read ("code block, 3 lines"), spoilers never read, runs of the same emoji and stretched words shortened, at most 300 characters. Your own messages are never read.
  • When. Only in the channel you have open, never while it's muted or set to "Nothing", in quiet hours, with do not disturb or in streamer mode. Switching channels stops it. At most five messages wait; older ones are dropped.
  • Nothing leaves the device. The text goes to the operating system's speech engine only. Voice, speed and volume are settings on the device.
  • Screen readers. A screen reader already reads new messages. A web page can't tell that one is running, so with one, leave "Read new messages aloud" off to avoid hearing everything twice.
  • Where it works. The web app and desktop app (Windows, macOS; Linux with speech-dispatcher) and iOS. Android's web view has no speech synthesis, so the options aren't shown there.

How transparent it is#

node scripts/audio-quality.mjs in client/ runs the e2e speech fixture (a real recording: a quiet room, noise floor around -42 dBFS) through the same code the worklets run, block by block, and compares what comes out with what went in (delay removed): clean, with fan and keyboard noise added (pink noise at -42 dBFS, clicks peaking at -16 dBFS), and 20 dB quieter. src/state/audio/quality.test.ts holds the thresholds, plus a golden-file check against DeepFilterNet's own command line tool (deep-filter 0.5.6: same output to within 16-bit rounding on clean speech, within 0.5 dB of its quality on noisy speech) and three minutes through the simulated worklet (every sample in order). Speech level is the median gain on speech, and its 5th percentile (the syllables turned down most); gain motion is how much that gain changes from one 10 ms to the next.

Input → stage Before: SI-SDR / spectral distance dB Before: speech level / dips dB Before: gain motion RMS / max dB After: SI-SDR / spectral distance dB After: speech level / dips dB After: gain motion RMS / max dB
Clean → AI noise removal 3.2 / 5.8 -9.5 / -4.0 2.47 / 9.9 20.6 / 5.0 -0.5 / -1.3 0.31 / 2.1
Noisy → AI noise removal 6.1 / 9.6 -0.8 / -11.2 2.53 / 9.7 19.7 / 9.0 -0.6 / -1.2 0.39 / 2.5
Clean → voice gate -1.2 / 6.7 0.0 / -16.8 2.31 / 14.7 > 99 / 0.2 0.0 / 0.0 0 / 0
Clean → leveling 10.4 / 2.3 1.4 / -4.3 0.59 / 4.1 12.7 / 1.7 4.2 / -3.7 0.23 / 1.5
Clean → whole chain -6.3 / 10.7 -4.1 / -13.1 3.13 / 15.1 11.2 / 5.6 1.9 / -3.8 0.35 / 2.1
Noisy → whole chain -5.1 / 14.1 -0.9 / -19.2 14.0 / > 99 11.5 / 9.3 1.7 / -4.1 0.41 / 2.4
Quiet → whole chain -5.9 / 13.2 -5.7 / < -99 7.6 / > 99 7.9 / 8.3 4.0 / -7.0 0.51 / 3.0
  • Audio dropped while talking (spread of the delay along the run): before 112 ms (clean) and 128 ms (noisy) through the gate; now 0. The gate's delay: before 250 ms, catching up by dropping audio; now 100 ms, steady.
  • Start of a word (the fixture cut into 17 phrases, clean and noisy): the voiced start always gets through. The faint lead-in is softened by (median / p95) 27 / 45 ms clean and 15 / 45 ms noisy with the 100 ms pre-roll; measured alternatives: 60 ms 67 / 85, 80 ms 47 / 65, 120 ms 7 / 25, 200 ms none. No clipped samples anywhere, before or after; input volume 200% is limited instead of clipped. The gate opens once on the fixture and doesn't chatter, before and after.
  • Noise removed (fan and keyboard, in the pauses, AI noise removal alone): 25 dB at Normal (30 dB limit), 17 dB at Gentle (18 dB), 32 dB at Max; before, everything (frames muted completely, speech too).
  • The whole chain's SI-SDR is lower than its parts' because leveling changes the level slowly over the run (it should); the spectral distance and gain motion show what it does to the sound.
  • What changed: DeepFilterNet's thresholds (the big one: clean speech was turned down by 9.5 dB, choppily, and some syllables muted), its strength limit, the gate (no more skipping), the leveler (RMS compressor, look-ahead limiter, gains that glide), and the gate's fade (it used to buzz faintly at half the sample rate while open).
  • Not measured offline: Opus itself (48 kbps mono for voice, with FEC, RED and DTX) and the browser's own echo cancellation and automatic gain.

CPU#

Realtime factor = time spent / length of audio (0.05 = 5% of one CPU core). node scripts/bench-audio.mjs in client/ measures them on any machine. On a desktop PC (2026, x64, Node 24):

Realtime factor
DeepFilterNet3 (your mic, or one incoming voice) ~0.07 (Chromium in the e2e tests: 0.05–0.12)
Silero VAD ~0.025
Leveling, per incoming voice ~0.004
Voice activity gate < 0.001

What the audio thread pays (same script: time per 128-sample render call, which has 2.67 ms; the speech fixture with noise):

Mean p99 Max
DeepFilterNet inside the render call (before) 250 µs 1.0–1.5 ms 3.7–7.0 ms
DeepFilterNet in a worker, the worklet only queues (now) 4 µs 10 µs 0.5–1.3 ms (first calls)
The worker, per 10 ms frame 0.95–1.2 ms 1.3–4.2 ms 1.7–45 ms (the odd pause: garbage collection, the OS)

In Chromium (the e2e tests) the worker takes 1.2–1.6 ms per frame on average and 2.0–2.6 ms at the slowest, with no late frames, for your mic and incoming voices at once.

DeepFilterNet's start-up takes about half a second (model loading); the first use downloads about 12 MB (16 MB WebAssembly and an 8 MB model, compressed). Phones are several times slower, which is what the automatic fallback is for. The app logs the realtime factor to the developer console every 10 seconds while AI noise removal runs.

Live captions (node scripts/bench-captions.mjs [file.wav], same machine): Whisper base takes about 2.0 s of encoder plus 30–50 ms per word, so 2.3–2.9 s per phrase whatever its length (Chromium: 2.4–2.7 s encoder); for the 8 s test phrase that's a realtime factor of 0.35, for a 1–3 s phrase 1 or more. In other words: captions arrive 2–3 s after someone finishes a phrase, and one desktop core keeps up with roughly one person talking continuously; with more, phrases get skipped. Loading the model takes about 0.6 s (Node) to 1.5 s (Chromium, from the cache).

Background effects (Chromium in the e2e tests, 640×480 fake camera at 20 fps, software WebGL): 8–15 ms per frame alone (segmentation about 10 ms, drawing 2–3 ms: roughly a third of a core at 30 fps), 25 ms per frame and 16 fps while a whole call, AI noise removal and captions run on the same machine. A real GPU makes the drawing faster; phones are slower, which is what the fallback is for.

DeepFilterNet's code was changed to build against tract 0.23 (client/vendor/deepfilternet/tract-0.23.patch; API updates only, the model is unchanged) and to let the app set its local SNR thresholds (wasm-thresholds.patch). scripts/build-deepfilter.sh rebuilds deepfilter.wasm bit for bit from the pinned sources, client/vendor/deepfilternet/Cargo.lock and Rust 1.99.0 (on any machine: local paths are mapped out of the binary); the "DeepFilterNet build check" workflow does that whenever any of it changes and fails if the bytes differ. The golden files in client/vendor/deepfilternet/golden/ are the official deep-filter 0.5.6 tool's output for node scripts/deepfilter-golden.mjs (see that script). Silero VAD's network is reimplemented in client/src/state/audio/silero.ts and reads the official model file; its output matches ONNX Runtime to within 1e-6.

node scripts/get-models.mjs (from the repo root) fetches Whisper at the pinned commit, checks its SHA-256 and writes the parts into client/.models/ (ignored by git). The e2e test servers serve the model from there (Captions.ModelSource) instead of fetching it from Hugging Face, and CI caches it. Without it, the Whisper unit test and the captions e2e test are skipped. --blur also re-checks the committed Selfie Segmenter. The background pictures are drawn in code; there are no image assets.

Voice bots (SDK)#

The bot SDK plays audio into voice channels with these packages. They're installed by npm install in bots/ (exact versions in bots/package-lock.json), loaded only when a bot uses voice, and never part of the app or the server.

Component Version Used for License
@livekit/rtc-node with @livekit/rtc-ffi-bindings (native, prebuilt for Windows x64, macOS x64/arm64, Linux x64/arm64; includes libwebrtc) 1.1.0 / 0.12.73 connecting to the server's LiveKit and publishing the audio track; resampling (AudioResampler) Apache-2.0 (libwebrtc: BSD-3-Clause)
mpg123-decoder (mpg123 in WebAssembly) 1.0.3 MP3 MIT; contains mpg123, LGPL-2.1
ogg-opus-decoder (libopus in WebAssembly) 1.7.5 Ogg Opus MIT; contains libopus, BSD-3-Clause
@wasm-audio-decoders/ogg-vorbis (libvorbis in WebAssembly) 0.1.20 Ogg Vorbis MIT; contains libvorbis and libogg, BSD-3-Clause
@wasm-audio-decoders/flac (libFLAC in WebAssembly) 0.2.11 FLAC MIT; contains libFLAC, BSD-3-Clause
codec-parser (used by the Ogg and FLAC decoders) 2.5.0 finding frames in Ogg and FLAC streams LGPL-3.0-or-later

WAV is read by the SDK itself (bots/sdk/src/voice/audio.ts). The LGPL parts are used unmodified, as the separate npm packages they ship in.

Rich text (code and math)#

Code blocks and LaTeX math in messages, threads, forums and docs pages. Both are bundled with the app (no CDN), loaded only when a message needs them, and their output is turned into React elements through an allowlist (client/src/ui/chat/safeTrees.ts), never inserted as HTML.

Component Version Used for License
lowlight 3.3.0 syntax highlighting as a token tree MIT
highlight.js (grammars, through lowlight) 11.11.2 the common languages, and guessing one for untagged blocks BSD-3-Clause
Temml (with its small Temml.woff2 font and Temml-Local.css) 0.13.5 LaTeX to MathML MIT
